text:
I've been quiet on here for a few months. Intentionally.

After 20 years moving fast in corporate product management, I stopped. Not because I had to — because I wanted to see what would happen if I actually made time to think.

Here's what happened:

I built a digital literacy platform for Canadian seniors from scratch. 167 pages. 19 modules. Bilingual. Accessible. In 72 hours of focused building.

I also built an AI job coaching tool. A rental search platform. A free business diagnostic for local SMEs.

None of this was on a roadmap. None of it had a budget. All of it had purpose.

I'm not going to pretend the gap wasn't scary at first. It was. But leaning into it — really leaning in — has been one of the most clarifying experiences of my career.

If you're in a gap right now: you're not behind. You might just be getting started.

And if you're looking for someone who knows how to build things that matter to real people — I'm open to a conversation.

→ aaron.patzalek@gmail.com
image_prompt: Aaron working at a desk, focused and calm — genuine, warm, not corporate. Natural light, coffee nearby.

text:
Day one of the gap felt like standing at the edge of something very large.

I had a list of things I was supposed to do. Update the resume. Refresh LinkedIn. Book coffees. Start the search.

I did none of them that first day.

Instead, I sat with the quiet.

That sounds either very zen or very avoidant, depending on your read. It was probably both.

After 20 years of being perpetually calendared — meetings stacked against meetings, decisions waiting for decisions — I had a day with nothing required of it.

I didn't know what to do with that. Not right away.

What I eventually did was make a list. Not a to-do list. A different kind of list.

What problems do I actually care about?
Who do I actually want to help?
What would I build if I knew it mattered to the right people?

That list turned out to be the most useful thing I wrote in the gap.

Not because it gave me a job. But because it gave me a direction. And direction, I've learned, is more valuable than a plan.

If you're at the start of a gap: resist the urge to fill the quiet immediately. There's something useful in it.

What's in the quiet that you've been too busy to hear?
image_prompt: Empty desk at a window, morning light, a notebook open but mostly blank — quiet and contemplative

text:
Week four of the gap was the week things changed.

Weeks one through three had been uncomfortable. I'd been productive — building, reading, thinking — but there was an undercurrent of anxiety that I kept talking myself past.

You're fine. This is deliberate. You chose this.

True. And also — anxious.

Week four, something shifted.

I shipped the first version of the Digital Confidence Centre. Sent it to a few people. Got a response from a woman in her 70s who said: "This is the first time a website has made me feel like it was built for me."

I sat with that for a while.

Not because it was flattering. Because it answered a question I hadn't known I was asking.

Am I still capable of building something that matters?

Yes. Obviously. But I needed the evidence.

The anxiety didn't disappear after that. But it became a different kind of anxiety — the productive kind that lives alongside ambition rather than against it.

I think that shift — from anxious-about-gap to energised-about-work — is the inflection point of every good career transition.

You don't always know when it's coming. But you recognise it when it arrives.

Where are you in your transition right now?
image_prompt: Person looking at a completed project on screen with a quiet smile — the moment of 'I made this' satisfaction

text:
What I discovered about myself in the gap that I couldn't have discovered in a job.

I'm a builder.

Not in a startup-founder-hustle-culture way. In the actual sense: I get energy from taking a problem that exists and creating something that addresses it.

I knew this about myself at some level. But inside a corporate structure, you're often building around constraints that aren't the problem — organisational politics, competing priorities, inherited technical decisions, processes that predate the problem you're trying to solve.

In the gap, I built without those constraints.

And I found out something important: I'm faster at this than I thought. More intuitive. More comfortable with ambiguity than the controlled environment of a large organisation ever required me to be.

I also found out that I do my best thinking when I have ownership over the question, not just the execution.

Not every role allows for that. But now I know I need to look for it.

That's not a lesson I was going to learn on a normal Tuesday inside Telus.

The gap gave me data about myself that years of performance reviews never could.

What have you learned about yourself that a job couldn't teach you?
image_prompt: Notebook with handwritten self-reflection, warm light — introspective and genuine

text:
What I'd tell my past self on the day the gap started.

Dear Aaron — six months ago:

You're about to have the most uncomfortable and most clarifying experience of your professional life. Here's what to know going in.

The discomfort is not a sign that something is wrong. It's a sign that something is changing. Those are not the same thing.

Don't fill the calendar to avoid the quiet. The quiet is where you'll figure out what you actually want.

You will build things you're proud of. Not because you have to. Because you want to. And that distinction will matter more than you expect.

The skills you developed over 20 years are not company property. They came with you. They are, if anything, sharper now that you're using them on your own terms.

Some people will look at the gap and see a gap. You'll know what it actually is: a period of purposeful building that produced more real output than many years of corporate effort.

And when someone asks what you did during this time — tell them clearly, without apology.

You built things that helped people. That's not a gap. That's the job.

If you're in a gap right now: this is for you too.
image_prompt: Letter on a desk, handwritten, warm and personal — advice to a past self, not a business document

text:
One thing the gap gave me that corporate life never could.

Ownership of the question.

In 20 years of product management, I owned answers. Roadmaps. Releases. Feature delivery. Stakeholder alignment.

What I rarely owned — fully, without a layer of organisational context shaping it — was the question itself.

What are we actually trying to do? For whom? Why does it matter?

Those questions existed. I asked them often. But they were asked within a frame someone else had set: the company's strategy, the quarterly OKRs, the inherited product vision.

In the gap, I own the question.

Why are seniors digitally excluded? What would actually change their experience? Is a platform the right vehicle?

Answering those questions without an organisation's gravity pulling my reasoning — without the need to align with what's already been decided — produced something different.

Not necessarily better. But more honest.

I've heard many people talk about 'entrepreneurial thinking inside large organisations.' I think what they're actually describing is this: the ability to own the question, even if you don't own the resources.

That skill is hard to develop when every question has already been partially answered before you arrive.

The gap forced me to develop it from scratch. That's the gift I didn't know I needed.

Have you ever had full ownership of the question?
image_prompt: Open road ahead, taken from driver's perspective — metaphor for owning the direction without a pre-set route

text:
Let me tell you what the Digital Confidence Centre actually is.

Not the elevator pitch. The real thing.

It's a free, bilingual, fully accessible digital literacy platform for Canadian seniors.

19 modules covering everything from the basics of using an iPhone to understanding AI, online banking, grocery delivery, ride-sharing apps, and how to protect yourself from scams.

167 pages of content written in plain language, tested for readability, designed for iPads at font sizes that actually work for someone over 70.

Fully bilingual — English and French — not as an afterthought but as a design requirement from day one.

Built on a static site that runs entirely for free on GitHub Pages. No server costs. No subscriptions. No paywalls. Ever.

I built it in a concentrated period of about 72 hours of actual building time, spread across a few weeks.

Not because I had unlimited capacity. Because I had clarity.

I knew exactly who it was for. I knew exactly what problem it was solving. I knew what 'good enough to be genuinely useful' looked like.

That clarity — more than any tool or technology — is what made it possible.

The platform is live. It's free. If you know a senior who would benefit from it, please share it.

If you're an organisation serving older adults in Ontario — I'd genuinely love to talk about how we can get it in front of the right people.

Link in my profile.
image_prompt: Screenshot of the Digital Confidence Centre homepage on a tablet held by an older adult — real product, real person

text:
I also built an AI-powered career coaching tool. Here's why it exists.

During my gap, I became acutely aware of something the job market doesn't talk about enough.

Getting past the initial screening process is increasingly an AI problem, not a human one.

ATS systems filter resumes before any human sees them. Generic interview prep tools give generic answers. And personalised career coaching — the kind that actually helps — costs money most job seekers don't have during a gap.

So I built something.

The Career Coach is a free tool that helps job seekers:
— Analyse their resume against specific job postings
— Identify alignment gaps before applying
— Practice interview responses tailored to real roles
— Get feedback on how their experience maps to what employers are actually looking for

It's not perfect. No tool is. But it's useful in a way that generic resources aren't.

Building it also taught me something: the hardest part of job searching for most people isn't skills. It's not knowing how to translate their experience into the language the market is looking for.

That's a solvable problem. Good product design makes it more solvable.

The tool is live. Free. No login required.

If you're in a job search right now — or know someone who is — it might be worth a look.

Link in my profile.
image_prompt: Clean screenshot of the Career Coach tool interface, with a job posting and analysis visible

text:
I built a rental search platform for a friend. Here's what building for a real person teaches you.

When someone close to you is struggling with a problem you know how to solve — you build.

My friend Kevin was relocating and dealing with the exact mess that rental searches have become: aggregated listings from multiple sites, inconsistent data, no clear way to compare options across the criteria that actually matter to him.

I built a system that scraped and organised listings from the sites he was actually using, filtered by his real criteria, and presented comparisons in a format he could act on.

Not elegant. Not generalised. Not a startup pitch.

Just useful. For one person. Right now.

Here's what that project reminded me that platform work sometimes makes you forget:

The best product you can build is the one that solves a specific problem for a specific person so completely that they don't need to think about it anymore.

Scale is a later problem. Usefulness is the first one.

I talk to a lot of people building products for enormous markets with unclear users.

Sometimes I want to say: start with one person. Build something they'd use on a Tuesday. Then figure out who else needs the same thing.

That sequence produces better products than the reverse.

What's the most useful thing you've built for one specific person?
image_prompt: Simple rental listing comparison interface on a laptop screen — practical, useful, no-frills

text:
I built a free business diagnostic for local small businesses. Here's why it matters more than I expected.

Small business owners in Canada face a very specific problem.

They are surrounded by generic advice — 'build your social media,' 'diversify your revenue,' 'improve your customer experience' — that doesn't connect to their specific situation.

What most of them actually need is someone to help them see their own business clearly.

The Clarity Tool is a free diagnostic that helps a small business owner identify:
— Their key growth bottlenecks
— Where their time is being spent vs. where it should be
— What to prioritise in the next 90 days
— Which generic advice actually applies to their situation

I built it because I kept having the same conversation with local business owners: they knew something was wrong, they had no shortage of advice, but they couldn't connect the advice to their reality.

The diagnostic is a bridge. It doesn't replace a consultant. But it gives someone the language to understand their own situation — which is the first step to doing something about it.

Free. No login required. Designed for non-technical users.

If you know a small business owner who's spinning their wheels right now — share this with them.

Link in my profile.
image_prompt: Small business owner looking at a diagnostic report on a tablet or laptop — engaged, thoughtful, in a real business setting

text:
The portfolio isn't a collection of projects. It's evidence of a way of working.

I want to be direct about something.

The things I've built in the last few months — the Digital Confidence Centre, the Career Coach, the Clarity diagnostic, the apartment search system — they're not random side projects.

They're a demonstration of how I think about product work.

Start with a real person who has a real problem.
Get clear on what changes for them if you get it right.
Build the simplest version that's genuinely useful.
Iterate based on what you learn from the real thing existing in the world.

Every project in the portfolio follows that pattern. Not because I planned to build a portfolio — I built things because they were useful to build — but because that's just how I work.

The result is: a career coaching tool that helped real job seekers. A digital literacy platform reaching real seniors. A diagnostic that helped real business owners see their situation more clearly.

Real users. Real problems. Real outcomes.

If you're looking for a product leader who can get from problem to shipped thing quickly, without needing a large team or a large budget — the portfolio is the pitch.

Link in my profile. I'm open to a conversation.

text:
What AI has changed about how I do product management — and what it hasn't.

I've been using AI tools heavily for the last several months. Primarily Claude. Across research, writing, code, design iteration, and content creation.

Here's my honest assessment.

What's genuinely different:

Research speed. Synthesising large amounts of information into structured insights used to take days. It now takes hours. The time I used to spend organising what I'd found can now go to evaluating it.

First drafts. Getting from blank page to workable draft — for specs, for copy, for outlines — is dramatically faster. The quality of the first draft is good enough that I'm working with material rather than building from nothing.

Prototyping. I can generate functional code for simple tools faster than I could before. Not production-quality code, but real working things to test assumptions.

What hasn't changed:

Judgement. AI doesn't know which problem is worth solving. It doesn't have product intuition. It can't tell you when something is missing because the user hasn't asked for it yet.

User understanding. Real insight about real users still comes from talking to them, watching them, sitting with the discomfort of what they can't articulate.

Decision-making. AI can surface options. It can't weigh them in the context of your organisation, your constraints, your user's actual situation.

AI is a powerful capability multiplier. It's not a replacement for the thing it's multiplying.

What's your experience been?
image_prompt: PM working with AI interface — person and screen in equal focus, collaborative feel rather than replacement narrative

text:
What AI can't replace — from someone who's been using it to build almost everything lately.

I want to push back on something I see in a lot of AI-in-product conversations.

The framing is usually about what AI can do. The speed. The output. The automation.

Less often discussed: what it can't do, and why that matters.

AI can generate. It cannot evaluate without criteria you provide.
AI can produce options. It cannot tell you which option matters to your specific user.
AI can write copy. It cannot tell you whether the message will land with someone who's afraid of technology and needs to feel respected before they read the first sentence.
AI can code a feature. It cannot tell you whether the feature is worth building.

The judgment layer — the layer that sits between 'this is technically possible' and 'this is the right thing to do for this user right now' — that layer is still entirely human.

In fact, I'd argue that the more you use AI to generate, the more important your judgment becomes. Because the speed of generation creates a risk: you can ship things faster than you can evaluate whether they should be shipped.

The skill that matters most right now isn't knowing how to use AI tools. It's knowing when to slow down and apply the judgment that no tool can replicate.

Do you agree? Where are you finding the limits of AI in your own work?
image_prompt: Human hand and AI interface side by side — complementary, not competing — thoughtful visual balance

text:
How I actually use Claude to build — and where I've learned to pump the brakes.

People ask me about my AI workflow. Here's the honest version.

Where I lean on it heavily:

First drafts of everything. Specs, copy, user flows, email sequences. I give Claude a clear brief and a real example of the user I'm building for. The first draft is usually 70-80% of the way there.

Research synthesis. 'Here are 12 sources on senior tech adoption barriers. What's the consistent finding?' This task would take me half a day. It takes 10 minutes now.

Code scaffolding. For static sites and front-end tools, Claude can generate functional starting points fast. I'm not a developer, but I can evaluate and iterate on real code with AI assistance.

Where I've learned to pump the brakes:

User understanding. I stopped using AI to 'simulate' how a user would respond to something. It's not the same as talking to a real person. Not even close.

Strategic decisions. AI is great at surfacing considerations. It will not tell you what to prioritise. That's your call, and it should be.

Tone calibration. For audiences with specific emotional needs — like seniors who've been made to feel technologically inadequate — AI-generated copy needs real human review. The gap between 'technically correct' and 'genuinely respectful' isn't AI-navigable.

The summary: AI is a fast collaborator, not an experienced colleague. Use it accordingly.
image_prompt: Laptop open to AI chat alongside a notebook with handwritten annotations — human and AI working in parallel

text:
What AI adoption actually looks like on the ground — outside Silicon Valley.

Most AI adoption narratives are written by people who work in tech.

I've been spending time with a different set of people: seniors in Ontario learning to use smartphones. Small business owners in St. Thomas trying to understand if AI applies to them. Job seekers using my Career Coach tool who've never typed a prompt in their lives.

Here's what AI adoption actually looks like outside the tech bubble:

It's confusing and it's fast. People who are still learning to use Google are being told they need to understand AI. The pace of change has overtaken the capacity to adapt for a significant portion of the population.

Trust is the barrier, not access. Most people I talk to aren't asking 'how does this work?' They're asking 'can I trust this?' That's a different question requiring a different answer.

The benefits aren't obvious without a guide. AI tools are genuinely useful for a lot of everyday tasks. But that usefulness is not self-evident. It requires someone to show you a before-and-after that's relevant to your actual life.

The people being left out aren't lazy or resistant. They're overwhelmed by a pace of change that doesn't account for the time it takes to actually understand something new.

If the tech industry wants AI to reach everyone — and there are real reasons that matters — we need to talk about this more than we talk about the next capability release.

What does AI adoption look like from where you sit?
image_prompt: Two images side by side: Silicon Valley boardroom discussing AI vs. a senior in a library trying to navigate a tablet — the contrast is the message

text:
AI for small businesses — what's actually useful right now, and what's hype.

I've been talking with local small business owners about AI since I built the Clarity diagnostic tool.

Here's what I've found.

What's genuinely useful right now:

Content drafting. Business owners who hate writing can now get a first draft of an email, a social post, or a newsletter in minutes. The quality needs editing but the blank page problem goes away.

Customer communication templates. AI is good at generating variations of standard messages — confirmations, follow-ups, FAQs. This saves real time for businesses without dedicated staff.

Brainstorming. 'I want to do something for customer appreciation month — give me 10 ideas under $200.' AI is genuinely fast and useful for this kind of creative support.

Summarising feedback. Paste in a set of Google reviews and ask for the top three themes. Fast, useful, actionable.

What's mostly hype for small business:

Automated customer service bots. The setup cost and the failure modes usually aren't worth it at small business scale.

AI 'doing your marketing.' You still need a human voice and real content strategy. AI can support it — it can't replace it.

AI insights dashboards. Only useful if you have the data infrastructure. Most small businesses don't.

Start with the simple use cases. They'll give you enough return to justify the learning curve.
image_prompt: Small business owner at a counter using a laptop with an AI interface — practical, real-world scene

text:
Why senior digital literacy matters — beyond the obvious.

The obvious reason: seniors who can use technology have access to banking, healthcare, government services, and family connection that others don't.

That's true and it matters. But it understates the issue.

Here's what I've seen building the Digital Confidence Centre:

Digital exclusion isn't a convenience problem. It's an isolation problem.

When an 80-year-old can't video call their grandchildren because no one ever showed them how, they see them less. When they can't book their own medical appointments online, they depend on others for something most of us take for granted. When they can't navigate basic government forms digitally, they're cut off from services they're entitled to.

This isn't inconvenience. It's diminished independence. Accelerated isolation. A narrowing of the world that compounds over time.

And here's what makes it particularly important: we're not talking about a fringe population. Over 7 million Canadians are over 65. That number is growing. And digital systems — banking, healthcare, government — are becoming digital-only at a pace that outstrips digital literacy among this group.

The gap is real. It's widening. And it has consequences for real people's real lives.

Building the Digital Confidence Centre was my contribution to closing it. It's not enough. But it's a start.

What role can your organisation play?
image_prompt: Older adult on a video call with family — genuine joy, real connection enabled by digital access

text:
What digital isolation actually costs.

We don't talk about this enough in terms of real numbers.

Social isolation among Canadian seniors is a public health issue. Loneliness is associated with a 26% increased risk of mortality — comparable to obesity and smoking. It increases the risk of dementia. It correlates with depression, anxiety, and a range of physical health outcomes.

And digital exclusion is a significant driver of social isolation.

When you can't video call. When you can't connect with community groups that have moved online. When you can't participate in the digital spaces where your family and friends increasingly live.

You don't stop being isolated because the technology is technically available to you. You stop being isolated when someone makes it genuinely accessible.

The cost of not doing this work isn't abstract. It shows up in emergency room visits. In long-term care placements that happen earlier than they should. In loneliness that shortens lives.

The Digital Confidence Centre is one response to this. Free modules. Plain language. Accessible design. No paywalls.

But the platform alone isn't enough. Organisations that serve seniors — community centres, libraries, health authorities, churches, care homes — need to be bringing this into their programming.

If you work for an organisation that serves older adults in Ontario: I want to talk with you.

This matters. Let's work together on it.
image_prompt: Older adult sitting alone at a window — quiet, but not hopeless — context for the loneliness data without being exploitative

text:
The political case for digital inclusion — that nobody in technology is making loudly enough.

I want to make an argument that I think gets insufficient airtime in technology circles.

Digital inclusion is a right, not a courtesy.

In Canada, access to government services is increasingly digital-first. Tax filings. Healthcare appointments. Benefits applications. Voter registration information.

If those services are moving to digital channels, and a significant portion of the population cannot access digital channels — that population is being effectively disenfranchised from services they are entitled to as citizens.

This is not a fringe concern. Over-65s vote at higher rates than any other age group. They pay taxes, contributed to the systems that now benefit others, and depend on those systems themselves.

The argument that they should 'just learn' misunderstands the problem. It's not about willingness. It's about access to the kind of patient, respectful, accessible digital literacy support that most of them never received.

Government has a role here. So does the tech industry. So do the organisations that serve these communities daily.

Free platforms like the Digital Confidence Centre are part of the answer. But they're not sufficient on their own.

If you work in policy, government services, or technology — this is a constituency worth thinking about. Not as a charitable impulse. As an obligation.

What would systemic digital inclusion actually require?
image_prompt: Government building or public service setting with an older adult in the foreground — civic and dignified, not clinical

text:
A call to the technology industry on senior digital literacy.

This is directed at the people building the technology that's changing everyone's lives — including the lives of people who didn't ask for it to change this fast.

You are building products that seniors need to use.

Banking apps. Healthcare portals. Government systems. Communication tools. Food delivery. Transportation.

Some of you have done extraordinary work to make those products accessible. Most have not.

I want to ask for three things.

First: include older adults in your user research. Not as an edge case. As a primary user group for any product that touches financial services, healthcare, or government. Because they use those products, and the design decisions you're making are affecting their lives.

Second: invest in plain language as a design requirement. Not as a nice-to-have. A requirement. Language that assumes familiarity with systems the user didn't build is a barrier, not a feature.

Third: partner with organisations doing digital literacy work. Libraries. Community centres. Senior care organisations. The infrastructure exists. The gap is resources and connection.

I built the Digital Confidence Centre as one small piece of this. I'm under no illusion that it's sufficient.

What's sufficient requires the industry — not just independent builders — to take this seriously.

If you're in a position to make one of these three things happen: please do.

And if you want to talk about how — I'm genuinely open to it.
image_prompt: Conference stage or tech environment with an older adult visible in the audience — the user you forgot to design for
